title: 'At an end': Court puts stop to legal fight over police officer's conviction
article: The reasons why a London police officer's second pitch to overturn a conviction in the death of an Oneida woman failed were outlined in a decision released Tuesday.

The Ontario Court of Appeal dismissed Const. Nicholas Doering's bid to overturn his conviction of failing to provide the necessaries of life in the 2016 custody death of Debra Chrisjohn after a brief hearing on April 19.

In a decision released Tuesday, the court outlined its reasons why Doering, 31, must serve the 18-month conditional sentence ordered by Superior Court Regional Senior Justice Renee Pomerance last November.
"The principle of finality must prevail in these circumstances," the Appeal Court said.

"As far as the Ontario courts are concerned, any issue about the appellant's guilt, conviction or sentence on the charge of failing to provide the necessaries of life to Debra Chrisjohn is at an end."
The decision halts some creative legal stick-handling aimed at quashing Doering's lone conviction that eventually came out of a high-profile 2019 trial.

Chrisjohn, 39, died while in custody at the Elgin OPP detachment on Sept. 7, 2016. Doering had arrested the mother of 11 in east London after she was found high on crystal methamphetamine and walking into traffic.

A day before, she'd been taken to hospital after being found in similar circumstances by another London police officer. Elgin OPP were contacted because they had an arrest warrant for Chrisjohn for breaching a recognizance order. They chose not to execute the order until she was cleared medically.
Chrisjohn eventually left hospital against medical advice and London police had no reason to hold her.

At trial, court heard Doering was dispatched to deal with her about 5:40 p.m. and confirmed there was still an outstanding warrant for her arrest. He contacted the OPP, then consulted with an EMS supervisor at the arrest scene about whether Chrisjohn should be taken to hospital.
The supervisor looked at Chrisjohn through the window of a police cruiser and, based on his answers, Doering believed there was no need to take her.
Doering met OPP officers at a Tim Hortons at 7 p.m. to transfer Chrisjohn to their custody. He told them she had been medically assessed.
Not long after she was placed in custody at the Elgin OPP detachment, Chrisjohn was found motionless and breathing heavily in her cell. She was taken to hospital, where she died.

Pomerance convicted Doering of criminal negligence causing death and failing to provide the necessaries of life. But the law doesn't allow someone to be sentenced multiple times for the same set of facts. Pomerance sentenced Doering to 12 months in jail for criminal negligence and stayed, or set aside, the second conviction.

He was the first Canadian police officer convicted of criminal negligence causing death, but not for long. In August 2022, the Ontario Court of Appeal quashed Doering's criminal negligence conviction, taking issue with Pomerance's conclusion Doering had deliberately misled the OPP when he said Chrisjohn had been medically assessed, but rather agreeing Doering believed what the EMS officer had told him.

But the Appeal Court upheld the failing to provide the necessaries of life conviction, calling Pomerance's reasons for finding Doering guilty "unassailable." The stay was lifted and sent back to Pomerance, saying Doering "must be sentenced" on that conviction.
Doering abandoned his leave to appeal the criminal negligence charge to the Supreme Court of Canada, while the Crown's pitch to challenge Doering's successful appeal was refused in October 2022.

The case returned to London, and in a legal twist last July, Doering's lawyer asked Pomerance to re-open the case so he could present further submissions about why Doering should be acquitted of the necessaries charge, asserting the stay only could be lifted in Superior Court, then suggested that since the judge had set aside the necessaries charge, she could hear more legal arguments.
Pomerance said she didn't have that jurisdiction and imposed the 18-month conditional sentence.
Doering returned to the Appeal Court, arguing the judge should have allowed the case to be re-opened and new arguments heard. The Crown argued the appeal had no merit and couldn't be re-litigated.
The Appeal Court agreed with Pomerance "that the case was being remitted to the trial judge for sentencing purposes only."

"This court clearly directed the trial judge to sentence the appellant. Unless she imposed a discharge, which she did not, she was required to enter a conviction, which she did," the Appeal Court said.
The Appeal Court added it already had judged the merits of the case when it struck down the criminal negligence conviction.

Both the application to reopen the case in Superior Court and the appeal "are impermissible collateral attacks on this court's order affirming the judge's findings of guilt on the failing to provide the necessaries count and this court's order that the appellant be sentenced for this offence," the Appeal Court said.
"The appellant essentially asks this panel to sit in review of the panel that heard the original appeal. We decline to do so."

The "obvious route" to challenge the necessaries conviction would have been to take it to the Supreme Court of Canada, but it was noted Doering's defence lawyer told Pomerance at the sentencing hearing "it would have been difficult to obtain leave to appeal in the circumstances."
"While that may well be true, it does not create any greater jurisdiction in this court to hear his appeal - again," the Appeal Court said.
